title: A God who suffers
hook: the cross says God is not distant from pain

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in the dark. Your line was even darkness can be prayed. Did you read it all the way to the last line? Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

"Jesus wept." In the King James Bible, that's a whole verse, two words long. He's on his way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, at the village of Bethany. Mary, Lazarus's sister, has just fallen at his feet, crying. The people who came with her are crying. John says Jesus groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and then he weeps. Here's the strange part. In the story, he's about to call Lazarus out of that tomb. He knows how this ends. He weeps anyway. Today: a God who suffers.

Start at the grave. Christians believe Jesus is God come in the flesh. So when he weeps at Bethany, Christians see more than a sad friend. They see God crying at a funeral. He doesn't give Mary a lecture on death. He weeps with her. Next, a line from Isaiah that Christians have read as a portrait of Jesus: "He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." Acquainted with grief. Not a visitor to it. A neighbor. Jewish readers read the passage differently, some as speaking of the people of Israel; Christians hear Christ in it. Then the cross. Yesterday's psalm ended in darkness. On the cross, Mark's Gospel says, darkness came over the whole land, and Jesus cried out the opening of another psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Some Christians say this is close to the heart of their answer to suffering, such as it is. Not an explanation, but God inside the pain. Theologians put this carefully, and differently. Some say God's own nature cannot suffer, and that Christ suffered in his human nature, truly, as one person. Others speak more boldly of the suffering of God. Churches hold these with care, and the block ahead won't settle it. But both point to the same picture: on the cross, God is not watching from far off. Last, the letter to the Hebrews: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." Touched with the feeling. The writer means Christ knows weakness from the inside. That's today's line: god in the pain. Not above it, explaining. In it.

Here's the practice: think of God beside someone in pain. Settle, and breathe. This time, choose someone you've never met: a name in the news, a stranger in a waiting room, a face you passed today that looked worn down. Picture them where they are. If you pray, picture God not above them but beside them: in the chair by the bed, at the kitchen table, weeping with them the way Jesus wept at Bethany. You can say their name to God, and nothing else. If you don't pray, simply picture them not alone, and hold that picture. The bell holds the time.
A God who suffers. The Christian belief that in Jesus, God weeps at a grave and goes to the cross: not distant from pain.
Your line: god in the pain. Today, when you see someone hurting, in person or on a screen, say two words silently for them: not alone. Day one thousand three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross in times of suffering, through crucifixes, icons of the crucifixion, Good Friday services and the Stations of the Cross, and some pray with Christ's own cry from Psalm 22.

notes: Divine impassibility versus divine passibility summarized in two sentences ('Some say God's own nature cannot suffer, and that Christ suffered in his human nature, truly, as one person. Others speak more boldly of the suffering of God.'); a theologian should confirm this is fair to Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant positions and ranks none.
Isaiah 53: Jewish readings (e.g. the servant as Israel) described briefly as 'some'; confirm it is fair and not used as a foil.
'Jesus groaned in the spirit, and was troubled' (John 11:33) paraphrased in the hook.
'Two words long' refers to the KJV verse John 11:35 as quoted.
Original συμπαθῆσαι (aorist infinitive of συμπαθέω) in Hebrews 4:15: confirm form and gloss.
The carry is lowercase 'god in the pain' exactly as the index; the voice speaks it as written. The index may want 'God'.

Editor pass: softened a sweeping 'for Christians' to 'some Christians say'; the practice now turns to a stranger, since days 1377, 1378 and 1381 also ask the listener to bring to mind someone hurting.

Audit (fresh reviewer): John 11:34–38: Jesus weeps after asking 'where have ye laid him?' and only then comes to the grave; hook, match and myth said 'standing near the tomb', now 'on the way to the tomb'.
